text.p: Bank of Queensland Ltd, which has rebuffed the Queensland state government's offer to join its planned state mega-bank merger, is still awaiting an answer to a proposal to buy back most of the government's 45 percent stake.
"They (the government) have not answered our proposal," the bank's chairman, Neil Roberts, told Reuters in an interview.

Roberts remained adamant that Bank of Queensland wanted no part of the government's plan to bring together government-owned Suncorp Insurance and Finance Group, Metway Bank Ltd and Queensland Industry Development Corp to create Australia's
fifth or sixth largest listed financial services group.

He also said he did not believe the Bank of Queensland was in play following this week's announcement of a A$2.65 billion proposed merger between fellow regional banks St George Bank Ltd and Advance Bank Ltd in New South Wales.
"(St George-Advance) is an interesting combination and will drive some synergies through, which is not as easy to do in Queensland," Roberts said.
"I don't think anything has changed (for the Bank of Queensland)," he said.
"We are set apart from the (Queensland government) merger plan but the merged group is sitting there with a buy-back proposition on the table," he said.
Roberts said the bank's offer to buy back 30 percent of the government's stake would cost about A$100 million at the current market price of the shares.
Most of the funds would be available from internal resources but the entire funding exercise would require some form of capital raising, Roberts said.
"Given our bank is not merging it makes a lot of sense for the government to run its holding down," Roberts said.
"The proposal is that the government sells back to us 30 per cent of the shares with the balance of our issued capital, 85 percent held by the public," he said.
"A buy-back is our preferred option. We are still discussing the issues with the (state) government)," Roberts said.
"Such a buy-back rationalises the oversubscription of capital while at the same time drives more earnings per share back into the capital base," Roberts said.
Meanwhile the bank, which is due to release its latest annual profit result for the year ended August 31 on Friday, had no acquisition plans of its own, Roberts said.
"We're very focused on our high-quality customers and not intending to move interstate," he said.
Bank of Queensland reported a 10.1 percent rise in net profit to A$22.67 million in the year to August 31, 1995.
